title: Associations Between Human Papillomavirus Vaccine Decisions and Exposure to Vaccine Information in Social Media
screen_reason: Self-reported exposure is measured by STANCE, not by veracity. The single exposure item asks whether parents saw any information about the HPV vaccine on social media, and respondents then classify it as 'completely in favor / mostly in favor / mostly against / completely against / a mix of both'. Nothing in the numerator requires the content to be false, misleading, inaccurate, fabricated, or from an unreliable source, and no ground truth of any kind is applied: a wholly accurate news report about a real adverse event would be classified 'against'. The paper's own measures section never operationalises misinformation (the word appears only in the framing, discussion and conclusion, and in a cited companion study about support for platform standards). Under the governing rule that the numerator must qualify on veracity (breadth = fabricated|false|misleading), an anti-vaccine STANCE share is not a misinformation-exposure share, so no eligible RECALL estimate exists. Judgement call: see missed_or_uncertain, which records the exact shares in case an adjudicator rules that 'information against HPV vaccination' should be treated as vaccine misinformation.
missed_or_uncertain: JUDGEMENT CALL FOR ADJUDICATION — the paper does report clean, well-denominated self-report shares; the only reason they are not extracted is that their numerator is stance, not falsity. If the adjudicator rules that self-reported exposure to anti-HPV-vaccine social media content counts as misinformation recall, the extractable rows would be (all United States, survey, data collected July-August 2019, denominator = 1,073 US parents of 11-to-17-year-olds who use social media, Qualtrics non-probability panel): (a) 5% saw information AGAINST HPV vaccination only -- 'Overall, 20% of parents reported seeing information in favor of HPV vaccination, 5% against HPV vaccination, and 12% saw a mix of information in favor and against HPV vaccination.' (Results, 'HPV Vaccine Information Seen on Social Media'), with Table 4 giving the underlying denominators 52/1073 against, 126/1073 mixed, 217/1073 in favor, 678/1073 neither; (b) 12% saw a MIX of in-favor and against; (c) 17% saw information against vaccination 'whether alone or mixed' -- 'About one-third (32%) of parents in our study had seen favorable vaccine information, which is almost twice as many who reported seeing information against vaccination (17%), whether alone or mixed.' (Discussion). Note that (c) is a cross-category sum reported verbatim by the authors, but its companion figure 32% conflicts with the results-section 20% + 12% = 32% only if 'favorable' is read as in-favor-plus-mixed, so (c) would need R8 care. Also NOT extracted, and not eligible on any reading: 37% (n = 395) reported seeing ANY HPV vaccine information on social media (no veracity or stance restriction at all); the Table 2 breakdown of the MOST RECALLED information type among the 120 parents who saw against-vaccine information (parents' stories 61/120 = 51%, news reports 21/120 = 18%, advocacy groups 14/120 = 12%) -- these are shares of a content-type taxonomy inside a stance-selected subsample, not falsity shares; the Table 3 engagement shares (read 68%, ignored 30%, commented 15%, liked 12%, reposted 10% among the 120 who saw against-vaccine content) -- these are engagement with, not prevalence of, the content, and again the sample is stance-defined; 61% HPV vaccine initiation, 22% delay, 17% refusal -- vaccine behaviour outcomes, not misinformation; and all odds ratios in Table 4, which are association statistics. Every third-party prevalence figure quoted in the introduction and discussion (45% of 2006-2016 Facebook posts against vaccination; 39% positive vs 25% negative tweets; 24% of news/lay-media tweets negative; 55% anti- vs 45% pro-vaccine Instagram stories; 41% and 58% parental exposure) is cited from other papers and is barred by R8.

rob.design: Cross-sectional web survey fielded July-August 2019 to a Qualtrics non-probability market research panel of US adults: 11,000 panel members invited, 6,470 completed the eligibility screener, 5,270 ineligible, 91 excluded for completing under two-thirds of the survey, 1,109 eligible completers, AAPOR response rate reported as 58%; recruitment stopped at 1,200; 36 non-users of social media dropped, giving an analytic sample of 1,073 parents of one 11-to-17-year-old. Exposure, information type, engagement and all three vaccine-decision outcomes are single self-report items with no record verification; delay and refusal were asked only of the 878 parents who had discussed HPV vaccination with a provider. No content coding was performed, so no intercoder reliability is reported; instrument validity rests only on review by four researchers for content and face validity. Non-probability panel, self-selection and recall are the main risks; the authors note temporality between exposure and vaccine decision was not established.
rob.item6_quote: The questionnaire assessed whether participants were exposed to information about the HPV vaccine on social media with 1 question (yes/no), "Have you seen information (e.g., stories, reports, videos, news, etc.) about the HPV vaccine on social media even when you were not looking for it?" Parents who reported seeing information were then asked to categorize it, with response options: completely in favor, mostly in favor, mostly against, completely against, or a mix of both.
rob.item10_quote: Overall, 20% of parents reported seeing information in favor of HPV vaccination, 5% against HPV vaccination, and 12% saw a mix of information in favor and against HPV vaccination.
